sections.html:
Iowa City is the Johnson County seat, on the Iowa River in eastern Iowa along Interstate 80, about 60 miles west of the Quad Cities. The 2020 count was 74,828 residents, fifth in Iowa, and the metro area holds more than 171,000. Coralville borders the city to the northwest, and University Heights lies entirely inside the city limits.

The University of Iowa, founded in 1847, shapes the housing market. Median age is 27.1, a sign of the large student population, and rentals sit next to owner-occupied houses throughout the older parts of town. Neighborhoods people mention often include the historic Northside near downtown, the Peninsula neighborhood and the east side.

Iowa City served as the first state capital from 1846 to 1857, and the Old Capitol, begun in 1839, is now a museum. For a seller the point is simpler: many houses are old. Find out the year yours was built before you talk with anyone, because that usually decides what an inspector or buyer looks at first.

Flood risk is real in parts of Iowa City, and the 2008 flood is the event buyers remember. Water passed the Coralville Reservoir's emergency spillway on June 11, 2008, and the Iowa River crested at a record 30.46 feet on June 13. Nineteen campus buildings were damaged.

The city requires a floodplain development permit in addition to a building permit for work in a flood hazard area. An elevation certificate is needed when a new structure is finished, when a remodel or repair costs 50 percent or more of the building's value, or when an addition increases floor area by 25 percent or more. New buildings must sit one foot above the 0.2 percent flood elevation.

The maps have changed too. New FEMA maps took effect in August 2025. Flood heights dropped along Ralston Creek, which could take some properties out of the high-risk zone, and rose along Willow Creek, which could add some. Buildings in the 1 percent zone need flood insurance if the loan is federally backed. Because the city takes part in the Community Rating System, policies there get an automatic 20 percent discount.

  • Check the 2008 flood layer in the Johnson County GIS viewer to see whether a parcel was under water.
  • Call Neighborhood Development Services at 319-356-5120 for flood status and elevation certificates.
  • Ask your insurer how the new map changes your premium before you list.

Rental owners must hold a city rental permit, and that includes owner-occupied homes with more than one tenant. A landlord who sells should confirm the permit status with Housing Inspection Services.

Bedrooms cannot exceed 35 percent of a dwelling's finished floor area, new bedrooms need at least 100 square feet and interconnected smoke alarms, and every unit door needs a deadbolt. The city also stopped allowing duplexes to function as one unit, so existing ones had to be permanently separated.

Continued complaints can lead to suspension of a landlord's permit under the city's Property Management Policy, whose review period has run 24 months instead of 12 since July 2018.

  • Gather permit and inspection records before you list a rental.
  • Resolve any open housing code notices, or disclose them.
  • Confirm the bedroom count on the permit matches the house.

sections.h2: Assessor, treasurer and the transfer tax
sections.html:
The Iowa City Assessor values houses inside the city, and the Johnson County Treasurer collects the tax. Residents outside the city limits deal with the Johnson County Assessor instead.

Real property is reassessed every two years, in odd-numbered years, with a January 1 valuation date. To contest a value, file with the Board of Review during April 2 through April 30. That window is fixed, and the board has no power to stretch it. The assessor's office answers at 319-356-6066, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

The treasurer is at 913 S. Dubuque Street, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., or at PO Box 2420, Iowa City, IA 52244-2420, phone 319-356-6087. The spring half is due March 1, and a penalty of 1.5 percent a month begins April 1. Owners must also tell the assessor if a homestead is sold, and new homestead applications are due by July 1.

At closing, taxes are normally prorated, and the buyer is credited for your share or you pay the treasurer. Deeds that carry value also owe a transfer tax, eighty cents for each $500 beyond the first $500 (Iowa Code 428A.1).

sections.h2: How does a cash sale work for an Iowa City house?
sections.html:
With no lender in the picture, an offer here does not hinge on an appraisal or a loan approval. For a house with student-rental wear, an open permit or flood-related repairs, that can shorten the timeline.

  1. Describe the house, its condition and any tenants or permits.
  2. Receive a written offer and decide.
  3. If you accept, a title company prepares the closing.
  4. Taxes and any liens are settled from the proceeds at closing.

You can decline and owe nothing. Before choosing, line the offer up against repair costs, inspection credits and the months a listing could take.

sections.h2: Selling a rental with tenants in place
sections.html:
Plenty of Iowa City sellers are landlords. A buyer is free to keep the tenants. The lease and the city's rental permit rules then carry into the purchase contract, so spell out who is responsible for what. Bring each lease, the permit and inspection records, and the deposit details to the table so the title company can account for them.

If you would rather deliver the house empty, agree on a move-out date with the tenants in writing and set the closing around it. In either case, confirm the bedroom count on the permit matches the house, because a mismatch is the kind of detail that slows a closing.

sections.h2: Preparing the paperwork for a quick sale
sections.html:
A little organizing helps an Iowa City sale move quickly. Start with the parcel. Look up the 2008 flood layer and the new FEMA map for your address and write down what each shows. Next, gather repair and insurance records for anything involving water, because buyers and insurers ask. Then collect the tax statement from the Johnson County Treasurer and, if you claim a homestead, remember that the assessor needs to hear when it is sold.

If the house has student-rental wear, be honest about it. Carpet, paint, appliances and wall damage are priced into a cash offer from the start, so there is less room for surprises after you accept. Having this folder ready also lets the title company move faster once you pick a closing date.

faqs.q: How many people live in Iowa City?
faqs.a: The 2020 count was 74,828 residents. The city ranks fifth in Iowa, and the metro area has more than 171,000 people.

faqs.q: Does Iowa City have its own property assessor?
faqs.a: Yes. The Iowa City Assessor values houses inside the city limits, while the Johnson County Assessor covers areas outside it. The Johnson County Treasurer collects the tax.

faqs.q: When can I protest an Iowa City property assessment?
faqs.a: You file with the Board of Review any time from April 2 through April 30 of the assessment year. Reassessment comes in odd-numbered years, and the board will not extend the deadline.

faqs.q: Do I need a rental permit to rent part of my Iowa City home?
faqs.a: Yes, if more than one tenant lives in an owner-occupied dwelling. The rental permit rules cover those homes along with other rentals.

faqs.q: Is Iowa City in a flood zone?
faqs.a: Parts of it are. The Iowa River flooded in June 2008, and new FEMA maps from August 2025 changed flood heights along Ralston Creek and Willow Creek. Check your parcel with Neighborhood Development Services.
